item.title: Signs that you might be impacted by the layoffs - Big Tech Edition
item.description: Layoffs in big tech rarely feel sudden in hindsight — the signals are almost always there weeks or months before the announcement.
item.dc:creator: Zalak Bhojani
item.content:encoded:
Subscribe now

Layoffs in big tech rarely feel sudden in hindsight — the signals are almost always there weeks or months before the announcement. Across ~4 years at AWS, I've been part of 3 different teams, all three of which were eventually impacted by layoffs. I've seen the same pattern play out with friends across other big tech firms too. This blog documents that pattern — not to make you anxious, but to make sure you're not caught off guard.

Note: This is written from the perspective of a mid/senior level individual contributor based in India. If you're located overseas, have been through something similar, and think there are angles I've missed — I'd genuinely love to collaborate and expand this.

The sections below follow a domino effect, starting from whether your site or team is at risk, all the way down to whether you personally might be on the list.

1. Leadership changes at the top

This is often the first domino to fall. A new VP or Director frequently means new priorities - and they often want to “make their mark” within their first 100 days. Restructuring and cost-cutting tend to follow quickly.

If your team or site gets absorbed under an existing VP or Director who has no prior presence in your geography (beyond your team), and there are no concrete plans for expansion, it may signal that leadership doesn’t prioritize maintaining a site there. This often happens when the previous leader exits due to a major strategic shift or misalignment in direction. Your team gets moved under the new structure temporarily, while leadership figures out the longer-term plan.

2. Hard Hiring Freeze With No Backfills for Critical Roles

Hiring freezes are a fairly common strategy for organizations moving toward a leaner structure. However, the absence of backfills for critical roles - managers, senior engineers - combined with high attrition (one or two team members leaving every month) is a stronger signal worth paying attention to.

This is typically followed by critical projects being moved back to the primary site under the rationale of limited resources. If this pattern repeats, your team may end up owning only maintenance-level work - the kind that can increasingly be handled with AI tooling - which raises a cascading question: do we need this many people here?

Sometimes this gets masked by consolidating other teams under the local site lead. But unless that comes with concrete product ownership and clear long-term plans, it may just be delaying the inevitable. When senior people quietly exit and their roles are absorbed rather than backfilled, that’s often a preview of a restructure. The reorg is the setup; the layoff is the follow-through.

3. Budget and resource signals

Training and development budgets quietly disappear. Conference approvals get denied, team outings get canceled, and small perks start vanishing. Open headcount gets quietly closed - not officially frozen, but those few open roles on your team just stop being discussed.

Cross-functional projects get canceled or put on hold indefinitely. If a major initiative involving multiple teams suddenly loses momentum, it often signals that leadership anticipates pivoting of the project or significant changes to the teams involved.

4. Organizational Silence and Vague Communication from Leadership

Your site is going through visible turbulence - reorgs, de-prioritized projects, rising attrition - but the response from senior leadership is minimal. AMAs are rare, and when they do happen, answers are vague and deflective about the future of the team or site.

Important org-wide meetings start getting scheduled at timezone-unfriendly hours. Some members who recently joined through a reorg don’t receive certain meeting invites. Leaders who once enthusiastically called out wins from your team go quiet in broader forums.

5. Shift from Innovation to Maintenance Work

Even after delivering on critical goals and building trust with leadership, your team starts getting handed non-critical projects. The exciting, forward-looking initiatives stop coming, and the team is largely left keeping the lights on.

This is one of the subtler signals, but it compounds over time: less strategic work means less visibility, which makes it harder to justify headcount.

6. Absence of Strong Advocacy from Within

There’s a pattern that’s easy to miss: teams that do good work but don’t communicate it upward are disproportionately at risk. When decisions are being made about where to cut, the teams with the loudest, clearest narrative of impact tend to survive — regardless of actual contribution. This isn’t a cynical observation, it’s just how large organizations work at scale.

This gap in advocacy usually traces back to the absence of a strong manager or senior engineer who actively builds visibility for the team - in leadership forums, in planning cycles, in cross-team conversations.

A quieter but telling signal: if promotion cycles are moving through the rest of your org, but a clearly strong teammate’s case gets stalled or rejected with vague reasoning, it often means leadership has quietly stopped investing in your team’s future. Promotions require sponsors who believe in the long-term presence of a team. When that belief fades, so do the approvals.

7. Behavioral Shifts in Your Direct and Skip-Level Managers

Managers are usually the first to know and the last to be able to say anything. What you’ll notice instead is a change in how they show up.

Skip-level 1-on-1s start getting pushed or quietly dropped. Your direct manager becomes harder to read - present in meetings but not really engaged, giving non-answers to straightforward questions about upcoming work or your role going forward. Career conversations stop. They used to push for things - resources, headcount, opportunities for the team - and that advocacy quietly disappears.

Watch for a specific calendar pattern: recurring “leadership sync” meetings with no agenda, or blocks of time that simply say “busy.” At this stage, managers are often being briefed on upcoming decisions, asked to evaluate their teams, or being trained on how to deliver difficult news. They’re not being evasive out of indifference - they’re often legally or structurally restricted from saying anything. But their behavior tends to reflect the weight of what they know.

If your manager, who was once your biggest advocate, starts feeling more like a bystander - that shift is worth taking seriously.

8. Sudden Urgency Around Documentation

Documentation is always good practice. The signal here is not the documentation itself - it’s the urgency and timing of the ask.

If you or your team are suddenly being asked to create detailed runbooks, map out processes end-to-end, or do structured knowledge transfers with no clear product rationale - someone is preparing for people to not be there. Organizations don’t invest that kind of time in continuity planning unless continuity is genuinely at risk.

In full site or team closures, a common pattern is that a small group of high performers is asked to stay on temporarily after the announcement - not because they’re safe, but because their institutional knowledge needs to be extracted and transferred before the site winds down. They’re later moved to an adjacent team or offered relocation. This is also why layoffs tend to cluster around half-year or annual review windows: the documentation and transition work gets rolled into a structured offboarding timeline.

If this kind of ask comes out of nowhere, without a clear project or system launch driving it, treat it as a signal.

9. Being Consistently Set Up to Fail

Things consistently go wrong in ways that point back to you, but the root cause is structural, not personal.

Missed deadlines caused by dependency teams not delivering. Scope that keeps expanding without acknowledgment. Being held accountable in broader forums for decisions that were made above you. Feedback that’s vague but pointed. These things happen on every team occasionally. The signal is when they happen repeatedly and specifically to you or your immediate peers, while the rest of the org seems to operate normally.

In a pre-layoff environment, managers are sometimes put under pressure to build a paper trail or rank their teams. It’s an uncomfortable reality of how large organizations prepare for reductions. You don’t need to become agreeable to the point of being a pushover - healthy disagreement and intellectual honesty are still worth defending. But the practical play is: raise concerns clearly, commit once a decision is made, and be deliberate about not being perceived as someone who is difficult to manage during an already unstable period. That perception, fairly or not, carries disproportionate weight when the list is being made.

10. Internal Transfers Being Quietly Encouraged

If your manager or skip-level starts casually nudging you toward internal transfer opportunities - especially unprompted and not tied to any conversation about your career goals - it may be less about your growth and more about the team anticipating a reduction. It's a nuanced signal, but worth noting if it shows up alongside other items on this list.

So, Where Do You Stand?

If you're seeing 1–3 signals, stay aware but don't spiral — these can exist on perfectly healthy teams. At 4–6, it's worth quietly refreshing your resume and reconnecting with your network. At 7–10, the pattern is real enough to act on: start interviewing, get your profiles updated, and make sure you have a financial buffer in place. At 10, don't wait for confirmation — move now.
And regardless of your count, remember that no single signal is definitive on its own. What matters is the combination and the persistence of these signals over time. Use this as a compass, not a verdict.

Closing notes

Layoffs are not a reflection of your worth. They are business decisions driven by strategy, market conditions, and priorities that are rarely within your control. Even strong performers get impacted.

The best thing you can do, regardless of where things stand right now, is to stay interview-ready - keep your resume updated, stay sharp technically, and maintain your network. Not as a reaction to fear, but as a professional habit.
